statements.quote: This first statistics chapter introduces the mathematical framework for reasoning under uncertainty.
The core idea: real-world data is not random noise; it follows **distributions** that we can model, sample from, and use to make decisions.
By the end, you will recognize the key distributions (Normal, Bernoulli, Binomial, Chi-Square, Zipf) and understand how **statistical inference** lets us draw conclusions from samples.
Artificial Intelligence is often described as “Applied Statistics”: at its core, every decision an AI makes is a calculation of likelihoods.
The frameworks below come from diverse origins — games of chance, mapping the heavens — and now enable machines to learn from data.
The goal of studying distributions is not to memorize them, but to understand how large datasets behave.
statements.section: Distributions

statements.quote: Real-world data rarely matches a theoretical distribution perfectly, but studying the distributions changes how you see the data: not as isolated points, but as a cohesive whole.
statements.section: Distributions

statements.quote: In practice, many real-world datasets approximate a theoretical distribution closely enough for the model to be useful, and the statistical methods applied to them remain reliable even when the match is imperfect.
statements.section: Distributions

statements.quote: Methods used here are also applied in many areas of Machine Learning, such as **initializing neural networks**, **generating synthetic data**, **modeling uncertainty in predictions**, and **optimizing algorithms**.
statements.section: Distributions

statements.quote: Understanding distributions is a foundational skill that bridges statistical theory and practical applications in AI and data science.
statements.section: Distributions

statements.quote: Recognizing these distributions in real-world data — from telescope photons to pixel intensities in medical imaging — lets machines model uncertainty.
statements.section: How knowing about distributions helps in developing AI systems

statements.quote: Most natural phenomena are not random noise but follow mathematical patterns; by recognizing a Gaussian distribution, an AI can separate meaningful “signal” from background noise.
statements.section: How knowing about distributions helps in developing AI systems

statements.quote: For example, in autonomous driving, a sensor must decide whether a blurred shape is a pedestrian or a lens flare.
statements.section: How knowing about distributions helps in developing AI systems

statements.quote: Knowing the distribution of typical sensor errors lets the machine make a calculated “guess” rather than stalling on an exact match: abstracting the data into a probability curve is the “extra level of indirection” that, as David Wheeler is credited with saying, can solve any problem.
statements.section: How knowing about distributions helps in developing AI systems

statements.quote: These distributions also underpin the “scaling laws” that drive modern large language models.
statements.section: How knowing about distributions helps in developing AI systems

statements.quote: As described in \citetitle{sutton2019bitter} by Rich Sutton, progress in AI comes from “general methods that leverage computation” rather than hand-coded human knowledge.
statements.section: How knowing about distributions helps in developing AI systems

statements.quote: When an AI is trained on vast datasets, it is essentially learning to map the distribution of human language; applications like predictive text and weather forecasting rely on the fact that the next word or the next storm front follows a predictable frequency distribution.
statements.section: How knowing about distributions helps in developing AI systems

statements.quote: Knowing these patterns lets developers make choices — from initializing neural networks to selecting training data — that match the variation actually present in the data.

statements.quote: A fundamental rule in machine learning: **never evaluate your model on data it has already seen**.
statements.section: Dataset Splits: Why You Can't Test on the Same Data You Trained On

statements.quote: This is why datasets are split into separate subsets:
statements.section: Dataset Splits: Why You Can't Test on the Same Data You Trained On

statements.quote: * **Training Set (typically 70-80%):** Used to adjust the model's weights.
statements.section: Dataset Splits: Why You Can't Test on the Same Data You Trained On

statements.quote: The model sees this data and learns from it.
statements.section: Dataset Splits: Why You Can't Test on the Same Data You Trained On

statements.quote: * **Validation Set (typically 10-15%):** Used to tune hyperparameters (learning rate, architecture choices) and detect overfitting.
statements.section: Dataset Splits: Why You Can't Test on the Same Data You Trained On

statements.quote: The model does not learn from this data, but it influences human decisions about the model.
statements.section: Dataset Splits: Why You Can't Test on the Same Data You Trained On

statements.quote: * **Test Set (typically 10-15%):** Held back until the very end.
statements.section: Dataset Splits: Why You Can't Test on the Same Data You Trained On

statements.quote: Used only once to report final performance.
statements.section: Dataset Splits: Why You Can't Test on the Same Data You Trained On

statements.quote: If you ever use the test set to make decisions, you are cheating, and your reported accuracy will be optimistic.
statements.section: Dataset Splits: Why You Can't Test on the Same Data You Trained On

statements.quote: **Why three sets?** If you tune hyperparameters on the validation set, information about the validation set “leaks” into your model choices.
statements.section: Dataset Splits: Why You Can't Test on the Same Data You Trained On

statements.quote: You need a third, completely untouched set to get an honest measure of generalization.
statements.section: Dataset Splits: Why You Can't Test on the Same Data You Trained On

statements.quote: In small-data regimes (e.g., medical imaging with only hundreds of samples), **k-fold cross-validation** is used instead, where the data is repeatedly split into $k$ folds, and each fold takes a turn as the test set.
statements.section: Dataset Splits: Why You Can't Test on the Same Data You Trained On

statements.quote: A model is only as good as the data it is trained on.
statements.section: Bias in Data: The Mirror of Society

statements.quote: If the training data contains historical biases, the model will learn and amplify them.
statements.section: Bias in Data: The Mirror of Society

statements.quote: This is not a bug in the math, it is a feature of the statistical learning process: the model faithfully reproduces the patterns it observes.
statements.section: Bias in Data: The Mirror of Society

statements.quote: **Common sources of bias in ML datasets:**
statements.section: Bias in Data: The Mirror of Society

statements.quote: * **Historical Bias:** The data reflects existing societal inequalities.
statements.section: Bias in Data: The Mirror of Society

statements.quote: A hiring model trained on historical hiring data will learn the gender and racial biases present in past decisions.
statements.section: Bias in Data: The Mirror of Society

statements.quote: * **Representation Bias:** Certain groups are under-represented in the dataset.
statements.section: Bias in Data: The Mirror of Society

statements.quote: A facial recognition system trained mostly on light-skinned faces will perform poorly on dark-skinned faces, as documented by \citeauthor{buolamwini2018gender} in \citeyear{buolamwini2018gender}.
statements.section: Bias in Data: The Mirror of Society

statements.quote: * **Measurement Bias:** The features used to represent the data are noisy or systematically wrong for certain groups.
statements.section: Bias in Data: The Mirror of Society

statements.quote: * **Label Bias:** Human annotators introduce their own subjective judgments into the training labels.
statements.section: Bias in Data: The Mirror of Society

statements.quote: **The technical consequence:** Bias in data leads to systematically different performance across subgroups.
statements.section: Bias in Data: The Mirror of Society

statements.quote: The model's overall accuracy may look good, but disaggregated by demographic group, it can reveal dramatic disparities.
statements.section: Bias in Data: The Mirror of Society

statements.quote: Detecting and mitigating these biases is an active area of research in **fairness in machine learning**.
statements.section: Bias in Data: The Mirror of Society

statements.quote: The theoretical framework underlying much of supervised learning was formalized by \citeauthor{vapnik} in the 1960s–1990s.
statements.section: Statistical Learning Theory and Vapnik's Contribution

statements.quote: His **Statistical Learning Theory** asks a fundamental question: given a finite set of training examples, how can we bound the error on unseen data?
statements.section: Statistical Learning Theory and Vapnik's Contribution

statements.quote: Three key concepts from this framework:
statements.section: Statistical Learning Theory and Vapnik's Contribution

statements.quote: * **VC-Dimension (Vapnik-Chervonenkis dimension):** A measure of a model's capacity or complexity.
statements.section: Statistical Learning Theory and Vapnik's Contribution

statements.quote: A model with higher VC-dimension can fit more complex patterns but risks overfitting.
statements.section: Statistical Learning Theory and Vapnik's Contribution

statements.quote: The VC-dimension of a linear classifier in $d$ dimensions is $d + 1$; for a neural network, it can be proportional to the number of parameters.
statements.section: Statistical Learning Theory and Vapnik's Contribution

statements.quote: * **Structural Risk Minimization (SRM):** Instead of minimizing only the training error (Empirical Risk Minimization), SRM minimizes a combination of training error and model complexity.
statements.section: Statistical Learning Theory and Vapnik's Contribution

statements.quote: This is the theoretical justification for regularization techniques like weight decay and dropout.
statements.section: Statistical Learning Theory and Vapnik's Contribution

statements.quote: * **The Bias-Variance Tradeoff:** Models with low capacity (high bias) underfit; models with high capacity (low bias, but high variance in predictions across different training sets) overfit.
statements.section: Statistical Learning Theory and Vapnik's Contribution

statements.quote: The optimal model balances both.
statements.section: Statistical Learning Theory and Vapnik's Contribution

statements.quote: A significant step toward reconciling this framework with practice: \citeauthor{petersen2024mathdl} (\citeyear{petersen2024mathdl}) derive generalization bounds from the covering number of the network class (Ch.\ 14) and show that in the overparameterized regime, small weights (as initialization provides) make the relevant function class Lipschitz-bounded independently of the parameter count — so the bound no longer degrades as you add parameters (Ch.\ 15).
statements.section: Statistical Learning Theory and Vapnik's Contribution

statements.quote: This is the theoretical content behind **“benign overfitting”**.
statements.section: Statistical Learning Theory and Vapnik's Contribution

statements.quote: **Why it matters for AI:** the t-test (and Welch's variant for unequal variances) is the workhorse of **model comparison** — "is variant A really better than B, or is the difference noise?" — and of testing whether individual regression coefficients are significant.

statements.quote: Every time a team compares two models on a holdout set, or decides whether a new feature "helps", this is the arithmetic doing the accounting, a century after it was invented to judge a handful of barley samples \cite{murtagh2024guinness}.
statements.section: The t-Test: A Dublin Brewery's Answer to Small Samples

statements.quote: And the Poisson connection is not coincidental: in 1907, "Student" had already published a counting-paper that unknowingly **rediscovered the Poisson distribution** you met earlier in this chapter \cite{student1907haemocytometer}.
statements.section: The t-Test: A Dublin Brewery's Answer to Small Samples

statements.quote: Testing a difference is only half the discipline.
statements.section: The controlled experiment: from scurvy to ablation

statements.quote: The other half — the one that actually *creates* trustworthy evidence — is **designing an experiment** that produces a difference you can trust.
statements.section: The controlled experiment: from scurvy to ablation

statements.quote: That design was invented in three stages, and each is a direct ancestor of something you do in ML.
statements.section: The controlled experiment: from scurvy to ablation

statements.quote: The first stage was the **control group**.
statements.section: The controlled experiment: from scurvy to ablation

statements.quote: In 1747, the Royal Navy surgeon James Lind split twelve scorbutic sailors on the warship *Salisbury* into pairs, each pair given a different treatment — one pair took two oranges and a lemon a day.
statements.section: The controlled experiment: from scurvy to ablation

statements.quote: Within days, one of them was fit for duty and the other "almost recovered"; the pair on cider also improved, but the four other pairs — vitriol, vinegar, sea-water, and a balsam-of-Peru/garlic/myrrh/mustard/radish mixture — showed no improvement at all \cite[Lind, *A Treatise of the Scurvy* (1753)]{lind1747scurvy} \cite{scurvy_wiki}.
statements.section: The controlled experiment: from scurvy to ablation

statements.quote: Nobody *proved* citrus cured scurvy (the sample was tiny), but the **design** — pair the patients, give different treatments, compare — is the exact shape of a control group.
statements.section: The controlled experiment: from scurvy to ablation

statements.quote: \marginfig{james_lind.jpg}{James Lind (1716–1794), whose 1747 scurvy trial was among the first controlled trials.
statements.section: The controlled experiment: from scurvy to ablation

statements.quote: Public domain (Chalmers, 1783).}
statements.section: The controlled experiment: from scurvy to ablation

statements.quote: The second stage, and the one that matters most, was **randomization**, and it came from \cite[Ronald Fisher, *The Design of Experiments* (1935)]{fisher1935design}.
statements.section: The controlled experiment: from scurvy to ablation

statements.quote: The problem Lind faced but could not fully solve: even with pairs, the two patients might differ in age, diet, or constitution, so *who* receives which treatment leaks into the comparison.
statements.section: The controlled experiment: from scurvy to ablation

statements.quote: Fisher's answer was to **assign treatments by chance**.
statements.section: The controlled experiment: from scurvy to ablation

statements.quote: Randomization does not remove hidden confounders; it *distributes* them across the groups on average, so the only systematic difference between the groups is the treatment itself.
statements.section: The controlled experiment: from scurvy to ablation

statements.quote: The book gave the null hypothesis its canonical exposition; randomization had already appeared in *Statistical Methods for Research Workers* (1925) and "The Arrangement of Field Experiments" (1926), and replication and factorial design were not new in 1935 (\cite{design_of_experiments_wiki}).
statements.section: The controlled experiment: from scurvy to ablation

statements.quote: The third stage was the **double-blind** procedure: neither the person giving the treatment nor the one receiving it knows who is in the control group, so that expectation — the experimenter's *or* the subject's — cannot tint the result \cite[the double-blind study]{doubleblind}.
statements.section: The controlled experiment: from scurvy to ablation

statements.quote: It matured alongside the first large **randomized controlled trials**, the 1948 streptomycin studies that set the template for medical evidence \cite[randomized controlled trial]{rct1948}.
statements.section: The controlled experiment: from scurvy to ablation

statements.quote: Now map it onto what you do.
statements.section: The controlled experiment: from scurvy to ablation

statements.quote: An **A/B test** — ship variant A of a page to half your users, variant B to the other half, compare the metric — is Fisher's randomization applied to software.
statements.section: The controlled experiment: from scurvy to ablation

statements.quote: And an **ablation study** — remove one component of the model and measure what the metric does — is Lind's control group applied to architecture: the full model is the control, the ablated model is the "treatment", and the question *is the drop from removing this layer real, or noise?* is answered by the t-test from the last section.
statements.section: The controlled experiment: from scurvy to ablation

statements.quote: The whole discipline of judging a model by **deliberately breaking it and measuring** descends, step for step, from a surgeon pairing up scurvy sailors on a warship.
statements.section: The controlled experiment: from scurvy to ablation

statements.quote: Real-world datasets are rarely perfectly Normal.
statements.section: The Statistical Soul: Dataset Distributions

statements.quote: * **Long-tailed**: power-law distributions where most values are small, a few are huge (income, city size, social network followers).
statements.section: The Statistical Soul: Dataset Distributions

statements.quote: * **Multimodal**: two or more peaks (heights of mixed populations).
statements.section: The Statistical Soul: Dataset Distributions

statements.quote: * **Heavy-tailed**: more extreme values than a Gaussian predicts (financial returns).
statements.section: The Statistical Soul: Dataset Distributions

statements.quote: * **Sparse**: many zeros, a few large values (word counts in documents).
statements.section: The Statistical Soul: Dataset Distributions

statements.quote: * **Discrete**: counts or categories, not continuous (clicks, votes, ratings).
statements.section: The Statistical Soul: Dataset Distributions

statements.quote: Recognizing the distribution of your data is the first step in choosing the right model.
statements.section: The Statistical Soul: Dataset Distributions

statements.quote: A Naive Bayes classifier assumes features are conditionally independent (often violated).
statements.section: The Statistical Soul: Dataset Distributions

statements.quote: A linear regression assumes Gaussian residuals (often violated).
statements.section: The Statistical Soul: Dataset Distributions

statements.quote: Knowing when these assumptions break down is essential in practice.
statements.section: The Statistical Soul: Dataset Distributions

statements.quote: In any natural-language corpus, the $k$-th most frequent word has frequency approximately:
statements.section: Zipf's Law: The Physics of Language

statements.quote: This is **Zipf's Law**, which Zipf had already described in 1932 (crediting Estoup, 1916); 1949 is the date of *Human Behavior and the Principle of Least Effort*, and Auerbach (1913) had noted the analogous city-size regularity (\cite{zipf_law_wiki}; \cite{zipf1949human}).
statements.section: Zipf's Law: The Physics of Language

statements.quote: For English, “the” appears ~7% of the time, “of” ~3.5%, “and” ~2.5%, and the 100th most common word ~0.05%.
statements.section: Zipf's Law: The Physics of Language

statements.quote: Zipf's law is observed in many seemingly unrelated domains: city populations, income, web traffic, and more.
statements.section: Zipf's Law: The Physics of Language

statements.quote: The mathematical reason is debated; competing theories include preferential attachment (“the rich get richer”), information-theoretic optimization, and self-organized criticality.
statements.section: Zipf's Law: The Physics of Language

statements.quote: For LLMs, Zipf's law has two practical consequences:
statements.section: Zipf's Law: The Physics of Language

statements.quote: * **Token imbalance**: a few tokens dominate training.
statements.section: Zipf's Law: The Physics of Language

statements.quote: Effective sampling and loss weighting must account for this.
statements.section: Zipf's Law: The Physics of Language

statements.quote: * **Long tail of rare words**: the model rarely sees most words.
statements.section: Zipf's Law: The Physics of Language

statements.quote: Performance on the long tail is consistently worse.
statements.section: Zipf's Law: The Physics of Language

statements.quote: The **Dirichlet distribution** (next chapter) is a natural prior over categorical distributions; on its own it does not reproduce a Zipfian tail.
statements.section: Zipf's Law: The Physics of Language

statements.quote: Below, we analyze the actual word distribution of \citetitle{nietzsche1883zarathustra}.
